analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 estate tax repeal permanent, so very large inherited fortunes would never be taxed.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 167 cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2001 tax law phased out the federal estate tax, which applies only to inherited estates above a large threshold, but the repeal was set to expire after 2010, bringing the tax back. This bill would cancel that expiration, making full repeal permanent. It was sent to the House tax-writing committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — only inherited estates above roughly $2 million per person (about $4 million per couple in 2007) were subject to the tax, so the benefit is concentrated at the very top of the wealth distribution.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes permanent, rather than letting them return after December 31, 2010 as scheduled under the 2001 tax law.
Applies to the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, eliminating federal tax on the transfer of large estates between family members.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through either lower government revenue or higher taxes and borrowing elsewhere; the cost is concentrated in the form of foregone tax on the largest inherited fortunes.

drawbacks.text: Permanent repeal permanently removes federal revenue from the tax on the very largest estates, increasing pressure on other taxes, deficits, or spending cuts that fall on everyone.
The tax applies only above a multi-million-dollar exemption, so the benefits go almost entirely to a small number of very wealthy families rather than to ordinary households.
The 2001 law's scheduled expiration was itself a budget-rule device to hold down the official cost of the original tax cut; making repeal permanent locks in the full, unbudgeted cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are narrowly targeted at heirs of very large estates, while its cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across all taxpayers. That asymmetry is the core objection an honest supporter would have to answer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled action on it, so it died when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kenny Hulshof introduced the bill on May 17, 2007, with 65 original cosponsors listed in the bill text.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the panel that writes tax law, on the day of introduction.
The bill accumulated 167 cosponsors — 149 Republicans and 18 Democrats — but the complete action record shows no further steps: no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers, in effect: the estate tax remained on track to return, keeping a tax on the largest inherited fortunes in place and preserving that revenue. Wealthy estates did not get permanent repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers kept the estate tax

industries.industry: Heirs to very large estates / wealthiest households
industries.note: Permanent repeal would exempt the largest inherited fortunes from federal tax. The gain accrues to a small group of very wealthy families, while the lost revenue would be borne broadly.

industries.industry: Estate planning professionals (estate lawyers, trust and wealth advisors)
industries.note: Permanent repeal would shrink demand for estate tax planning and trust services built around the tax. Their interest in keeping the tax runs against the (mostly wealthy) clients who would benefit from repeal.
Repeal would permanently remove estate tax revenue, leaving other taxes, deficits, or cuts to make up the difference.
